f1_names: **Official Korean disease name: unverified (unresolved).** The National Institute of Crop Science series variety paper uses "northern corn leaf blight" ([KJBS Shin Topok 2017](https://www.koreabreedjournal.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.9787%2FKJBS.2017.49.2.109), disease resistance paragraph; [KJBS Hwang Da-ok 2019](https://www.koreabreedjournal.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.9787%2FKJBS.2019.51.2.105)), 2022 plant disease research review) uses "Northen Leaf Blight" Write ([RPD 2022 28(4):195](https://www.online-rpd.org/upload/pdf/RPD-2022-28-4-195.pdf), Introduction). The *E. turcicum* disease page was not found in Nongsaro (searching for codes D00001192 to D00001199), and the List of Plant Diseases in Korea online database returned an error. It is inaccurate to group this disease into the brown spot series as the user lists (pathogen is a different genus/species). The notation "northern corn leaf blight" in the quarantine note is a working label and not the basis for the official name. EPPO Priority Name: *Exserohilum turcicum* (Passerini) K.J. Leonard & E.G. Suggs (SETOTU), synonym is *Setosphaeria turcica*, *Trichometasphaeria turcica*, *Helminthosporium turcicum*, *Bipolaris turcica*, *Drechslera turcica*, English name is northern corn leaf blight, leaf blight of maize/sorghum ([EPPO SETOTU](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SETOTU), Overview).
f2_parts_stages: Symptoms usually appear from V10 to V14 to R6, and if there is a lesion before or after VT, the risk is up to 50% in susceptible breeds, and progression after R4 has little effect ([CPN NCLB Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight), Yield loss·Symptoms). It starts on the lower leaves and lesions also appear on the ear husk, but the grain is not infected ([CPN Encyclopedia NCLB](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/northern-corn-leaf-blight-of-corn), Symptoms).
f3_symptoms: Early lesions are water-soaked ovals with fuzzy edges, parallel to the leaf veins, and as they grow, they become cigar-shaped, up to about 15 cm (1-6 in)**, crossing the leaf veins. Mature lesions are gray to tan, and when wet, dark gray spores appear mainly on the underside of the leaf, giving them a "dirty gray" appearance ([CPN NCLB Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight); [CPN Encyclopedia NCLB](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/northern-corn-leaf-blight-of-corn)). In *Ht* gene cultivars or partially resistant cultivars, lesions become small chlorotic linear stripes and spores are rare (same source).
f4_confusions: Goss's wilt is characterized by water-soaked initial lesions, dark freckling, and sheen of bacterial exudate. Diplodia leaf streaks have concentric circles and pepper-like pycnidia. Southern corn leaf blight (SCLB) is a small rectangular lesion with a brown border and yellow halo that resides in the lower leaves. **It is similar to the NCLB resistance response type and may require laboratory diagnosis** ([CPN NCLB Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight), Diseases that may be confused). Stewart's wilt is a wavy edge stripe that starts from the rice leaf beetle's black marks ([CPN Stewart's](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/stewarts-disease-of-corn)).) Differentiation data from nutritional deficiency, herbicide phytotoxicity, and wilt are unsecured.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Lesion length and cigar shape, whether it exceeds the leaf veins, no water marks, freckles, or luster (suggesting absence of Goss’s wilt), no peppery spots (suggesting absence of Diplodia leaf streak), and origin of lower leaves. Dark gray-green spores in the center of the lesion can be seen with a smartphone camera or magnifying glass **x20 magnification**, and are easily visible after dew or rain ([CPN NCLB Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight), Scouting). It is difficult to distinguish between resistance-responsive type and SCLB based on photos alone.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* x20 close-up photo after dew, continuous cropping/conservation tillage, variety (*Ht* availability).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Referral to a diagnostic laboratory is recommended to differentiate SCLB from resistant response type (same source). There are at least 4 races, including race 1 ([CPN Encyclopedia NCLB](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/northern-corn-leaf-blight-of-corn), Disease cycle). The standard values for conidium measurement, culture, and PCR are unverified.
f6_conditions: Infection requires 6 hours of leaf wetness and is favored by 18–27 °C (64–81 °F). Lesions can appear within a week under favorable conditions; hot, dry weather slows development. The pathogen overwinters in residue, making continuous corn and conservation tillage risk factors, but spores move between fields, so rotation and tillage alone are insufficient (CPN). UMN lists 64–80 °F and prolonged wetness; only a search snippet was accessible in the original research (full text HTTP 403). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight) [Source 2](https://extension.umn.edu/agriculture/crop-production/corn/northern-corn-leaf-blight)
f7_occurrence: Korea: National Institute of Crop Science Field resistance evaluation of northern corn leaf blight of cultivated varieties has been reported, assuming domestic field occurrence ([KJBS Shin Topaz 2017](https://www.koreabreedjournal.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.9787%2FKJBS.2017.49.2.109); [KJBS Hwang Da-ok 2019](https://www.koreabreedjournal.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.9787%2FKJBS.2019.51.2.105)).) Domestic review also introduces it as a major disease ([RPD 2022](https://www.online-rpd.org/upload/pdf/RPD-2022-28-4-195.pdf)). The first recorded document in Korea is It is unverified. Overseas: CPN writes that, contrary to its name, it can also be severe in the southeastern United States ([CPN NCLB Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight)). EPPO distribution page is 404, CABI is unverified).
f8_quarantine: Korea: **not listed(check)**; In the regulated quarantine pest, there are only other species such as *Exserohilum holmii*, *Setosphaeria pedicellata*, and *S. rostrata* ([KR-Notice Annex 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519059)). EPPO: No Categorization item ([EPPO SETOTU](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SETOTU/categorization)). EU·China·Japan: not listed(verified)([EU-2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02019R2072-20261015); [CN](https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/files/reportingobligation/2025/01/07/CATALOGUE_OF_QUARANTINE_PESTS_FOR_IMPORT_PLANTS_TO_THE_PEOPLES_REPUBLIC_OF_CHINA_updated_20241128.doc); [JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). US: unverified(APHIS list inaccessible). Australia: unverified.

f1_names: The Korean name in Nongsaro corresponds to southern corn leaf blight; its listed English names include seedling blight and southern corn leaf blight. Nongsaro gives *Cochliobolus heterostrophus* as the pathogen. The Korean disease label is also used for rice brown spot caused by *B. oryzae*, so the crop must be specified; the two diseases must not be given the same English name. EPPO's preferred name is *Bipolaris maydis* (Nisikado & Miyake) Shoemaker (COCHHE); synonyms are *Cochliobolus heterostrophus*, *Drechslera maydis*, *Helminthosporium maydis*, and *Ophiobolus heterostrophus*. Races O and T are described. [Source 1](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/COCHHE)
f2_parts_stages: Race O mainly invades leaves, race T mainly affects leaves, husk, stem, leaf sheath, ear shank, ear, and cob, and infected seedlings often dry out ([CPN Encyclopedia SCLB](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/southern-corn-leaf-blight-of-corn), Symptoms). Infected seedlings may wilt and die 3 to 4 weeks after sowing, and early leaf infection can easily lead to stem rot ([Nongsaro D00001196](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202), Symptom Description). In Korea, it mainly occurs in the high temperature and humidity inland from **June to August**, and also occurs in early sowing tunnel cultivation in Jeju ([RDA press release 2025-06-16](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000803185), southern corn leaf blight paragraph). V/R step-by-step technology is unverified.
f3_symptoms: Small light brown spots spread between the leaf veins and are numerous **about 0.5 cm wide and 1~2 cm long**. Race T lesions are yellowish brown 0.6~1.2 × 0.6~2.7 cm and may be spindle-shaped with yellowish green/white interstitials. In later stages, the edges are dark brown to reddish brown. Infected grains are covered with black mold ([Nongsaro D00001196](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202), symptom description). CPN describes race O lesions as “tan, somewhat rectangular” with a reddish-brown border, and race T leaf lesions as approximately 0.6 to 1.3 × 0.6 to 1.9 cm rectangular to oval in shape with a chlorosis zone ([CPN Encyclopedia SCLB](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/southern-corn-leaf-blight-of-corn)).
f4_confusions: NCLB and its resistant reactive forms may require laboratory diagnosis ([CPN NCLB Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-northern-corn-leaf-blight)). gray leaf spot (GLS)) Mature lesions are rectangular, blunt-ended, limited to leaf veins, approximately 5 mm wide and up to approximately 7 cm long ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Symptoms). The contrast that GLS is longer, narrower and has parallel edges is an inference from comparing the two sources. Eyespot (*Kabatiella zeae*) has circular spots with brown rings and yellow halo and is abundant in cool temperatures (based on search snippets) ([CPN Eyespot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/eyespot-of-corn)).) Source of differentiation from abiotic disturbances is unverified.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Long oval to rectangular lesion limited between leaf veins, reddish brown/dark border, yellow halo, lower leaf distribution, ear/husk lesion (suggests race T). Since it cannot be distinguished from GLS or NCLB based on size alone, the border color and leaf vein localization pattern are also examined.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Cultivar cytoplasm type (T-type cytoplasm or not), seed source, spike damage, and continuous cropping.
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* **Race O and race T are difficult to distinguish from normal cytoplasmic corn only by symptoms**, and race T shows pathogenicity in the Tm-sc gene corn ([Nongsaro D00001196](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202), occurrence environment). The race identification protocol (differential host·molecule) and definitive differentiation procedure from NCLB response type are unverified.
f6_conditions: Damage is greater in **warm and humid climates of 20~30℃**, and if conditions are right, the outbreak is completed in about 60~72 hours. It overwinters in residues and infected grains and is spread by wind and rainwater. T race occurs frequently in northern regions and is rare in the dry season ([Nongsaro D00001196](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202), pathogen/environment). It is consistent with the inland occurrence from June to August in Korea ([RDA 2025-06-16](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000803185)).) The leaf wetting time value is unverified.
f7_occurrence: Korea: It is registered in the Nongsaro·NCPMS DB, the RDA 2025 press release mentions the occurrence in inland and Jeju, and the resistance of domestically grown varieties was also evaluated ([Nongsaro D00001196](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001196&menuId=PS00202); [RDA 2025](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000803185); [KJBS New Topaz 2017](https://www.koreabreedjournal.org/journal/view.php?doi=10.9787%2FKJBS.2017.49.2.109)). race The domestic distribution of O/T is unverified. Overseas: EPPO is written as “Present, no details” for South Korea and North Korea, “Present, restricted distribution” for China, and “Present” for Japan ([EPPO COCHHE distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/COCHHE/distribution)).
f8_quarantine: Korea: **regulated non-quarantine pest** — Notification Annex 3 “1. Cereal seeds e. corn" No. 1 "brown spot *Cochliobolus heterostrohpus*" (same as original spelling), same space as No. 2 and 3, maximum limit of inbred line·breeder seed 2.0% / hybrid·certified seed 5.0%, other diseases ([KR-Notice Annex 3](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519071)). EPPO: **Past A1/A2 (listed in 1975, Deleted 1981)**, not currently listed by EPPO; country entries are: Egypt RNQP, Uzbekistan, Azerbaijan, Georgia A1, Belarus and Moldova QP, PPPO A2 ([EPPO COCHHE](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/COCHHE/categorization)). kr_quarantine: *C. zeae-maydis* regulated quarantine pest; *C. zeina* not listed
f1_names: **Official Korean name: unverified.** No Korean name, including “gray leaf spot,” has been confirmed by authoritative sources. In the RDA 2025 press release, the description of "spotted disease" (gray to yellowish brown rectangular symptom, rare in the past, infection caused by soil spores splashed with rainwater) is similar to GLS, but the response cannot be confirmed due to the lack of a scientific name ([RDA press release 2025-06-16](https://www.rda.go.kr/board/board.do?mode=view&prgId=day_farmprmninfoEntry&dataNo=100000803185), spotted disease paragraph). EPPO is *Cercospora zeae-maydis* Tehon & E.Y. Daniels (CERCZM), carrying the English name gray leaf spot of maize ([EPPO CERCZM](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CERCZM)). ***C. zeina*** Crous & U. Braun (MB500863) is the existing 'Group II', and *C. zeae-maydis* is 'Group I', and it was confirmed that they are a separate species based on the ITS, EF-1α, histone H3, actin, and calmodulin sequences ([Crous et al. 2006, Studies in Mycology 55](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/), Abstract·Taxonomy). GLS is a complex disease of two closely related species, and *C. zeina* is dominant in some subtropical regions of South Africa and China ([Li et al. 2026, J. Fungi 12(9):650](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13608403/), Introduction).
f2_parts_stages: It first appears in the lower leaves 2-3 weeks before heading ([CPN Encyclopedia GLS](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gray-leaf-spot-of-corn)). Yield loss mainly occurs when the 8-9 leaves above the spike (supplying more than 75% of the spike's carbohydrates) are infected, stem infection causes lodging, and chlorosis appears about 9 days after infection ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Symptoms·Yield loss).
f3_symptoms: Initially, brown and tan spots (0.2 in wide, 0.4 to 0.8 in long) fill the space between leaf veins, and yellow borders are **visible in backlight**. Mature lesions are limited to the leaf veins and are rectangular, blunt-tipped, tan to gray, up to 0.2 in wide and up to 2.8 in long. Gray spores appear, which is where the disease name comes from ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Symptoms). *C. zeina* lesions are bilateral, 2-3 mm wide, 5-40 mm long, light gray to light brown ([Crous et al. 2006](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/), *C. zeina* description).
f4_confusions: Early GLS is most confused with anthracnose (*Colletotrichum graminicola*), eyespot (*Kabatiella zeae*), and early common rust pustules (*Puccinia sorghi*). Common rust pustules can be seen when enlarged, and spores come out when bursting. Mature lesions are distinct, but early lesions “can be easily confused” ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Similar diseases). For the difference from SCLB, see Section 14 ④. Data for identifying abiotic disorders such as potassium deficiency and phytotoxicity are unsecured.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Parallel rectangles limited to leaf veins, blunt tips, yellow border when backlit (early), progression from lower to upper leaves, gray spore layer. **It is impossible to distinguish between the two species through photographs.**
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Backlit photos, photos of leaves above and below the ears, continuous cropping, no-till, and surface residue coverage.
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* *C. zeae-maydis* grows faster in culture, produces cercosporin, and has longer conidiophores (up to 180 µm). *C. zeina* grows more slowly, has shorter conidiophores (up to 100 µm), and lacks the red pigment associated with cercosporin. Conidial sizes overlap. A histone-H3-based species-specific PCR assay has been developed (Crous et al. 2006). The original Korean regulatory research listed *C. zeae-maydis* only, making species identification important for quarantine decisions. [Source 1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/)
f6_conditions: **70~90 °F** (The original text was written together as "25~32 °C", but 70 °F is about 21 °C, so there is a possibility of conversion error, so it should be read as about 21~32 °C based on the original value of °F), with dew, rain, and irrigation **Free water for at least 12 hours, RH 90% or more**; Susceptible cultivars have an infection cycle of 14 to 21 days, conidium invades in 4 to 7 days, and up to 5,000 spores per 1 mm² lesion ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view), Disease cycle). It rarely survives in buried remains, and if more than 30% of the previous year's infected field surface remains, the likelihood of damage is high, and even 10% can cause significant losses. In Iowa, when reduced-tillage area increased from 55.1% to 77.9% from 1983 to 1997, the severity increased from 10% to 95% (same source, Residue/tillage). Reduced tillage, susceptible varieties, dense planting, and climate warming promote GLS ([Li et al. 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13608403/), Introduction).
f7_occurrence: Korea: **Domestic occurrence record unverified.** No domestic GLS report was found through PubMed and Korean searches, and the domestic record of *C. zeina* is also unverified. Crous et al. Korea is not included in the 2006 distribution list of the two species ([Crous et al. 2006](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2104713/), Distribution). The fact that there is a *C. zeina* dominant area in neighboring China does not mean its domestic presence. Overseas: *C. zeae-maydis* is for Azerbaijan, Brazil, Cameroon, Canada, China, Colombia, USA, Zambia, Zimbabwe, etc., *C. zeina* is for South Africa, Uganda, USA (NC·NY·OH·VA), Zambia, Zimbabwe (Crous et al. 2006). GLS was first reported in the United States and then spread to Africa, Brazil, and China ([Li et al. 2026](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC13608403/)). EPPO distribution page was 404.
f8_quarantine: Korea: ***C. zeae-maydis* regulated quarantine pest** (Notice Annex 2 "1. pathogen fungi *Cercospora zeae-maydis* Tehon & E. Y. Daniels"); ***C. zeina* is not listed (check)** (no separate description) ([KR-Notice Annex 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519059)). EPPO: Neither species has a Categorization item ([EPPO CERCZM](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CERCZM/categorization); [EPPO CERCZN](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CERCZN/categorization)). f1_names: The official name in Korea is **common rust** (銹病, Rust), and Nongsaro writes the pathogen as *Puccinia sorghi*. The crop name is not specified on the page, but the code is right after corn brown spot (D00001196) ([Nongsaro D00001197](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001197&menuId=PS00202), diseased myeongran·pathogen). EPPO carries *Puccinia sorghi* Schweinitz (PUCCSO), synonym *P. maydis*, *P. zeae*, and common rust of maize ([EPPO PUCCSO](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PUCCSO), Overview). It is a heterologous parasitic fungus that uses Oxalis* as an intermediate host ([Lee et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Introduction).
f2_parts_stages: It often begins in the late vegetative growth period (southern rust is after VT) and occurs on both sides of leaves ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Table 1). Husk·leaf sheath·stem can also be infected ([CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-rust-of-corn)). Domestic *P. sorghi* specimens were collected in late fall (October-November) ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.3).
f3_symptoms: Small yellow spots develop into powdery **brick-colored pustules (about 1/8 in, about 3 mm)** that are scattered or gathered together, and appear black when aged ([CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-rust-of-corn)). Reddish-brown pustules are scattered **both front and back of the leaf** and do not penetrate the leaf (in contrast to tar spots) ([Cornell Common Rust](https://www.vegetables.cornell.edu/pest-management/disease-factsheets/common-rust-of-sweet-corn), Fig. 1). In domestic specimens, uredinia (reddish-brown, oblong) and telia (dark-brown spindle-shaped to linear) were present on both sides of the leaf ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.1 Fig. 2A–J). Nongsaro describes it as “yellow to orange green spores on the back of the leaf,” which is different from the description of brick color and both sides in the English material, so rechecking the original text is necessary ([Nongsaro D00001197](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00001197&menuId=PS00202), symptom description).
f4_confusions: Comparison of CPN with southern rust: southern rust has orange to light brown pustules densely, almost all of them on the front, and starts after VT; common rust has brick-colored to brown pustules that are not dense and occurs on both sides, and begins the late vegetative growth period; The two common rusts can occur together on the same plant ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Table 1). Similar symptoms include Physoderma brown spot, eyespot, Curvularia leaf spot, tar spot, **genetic disorders**, and mite damage (same document, Fig. 8–13). Early pustules are confused with GLS early lesions ([UNL NebGuide G1902](https://extensionpubs.unl.edu/publication/g1902/html/view)).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Brick-colored pustules, bifacial/scattered distribution, low density, non-penetrating leaves (excluding tar spots), time of occurrence. **In Korea, *P. polysora* also frequently forms uredinia on both sides of the leaves, making the 'both sides = common rust' standard less reliable** ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Discussion second paragraph). Since the majority of recent samples in Korea were *P. polysora*, there is a high risk of misdiagnosis if it is determined to be *P. sorghi* based on photos alone.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Close-up photos of the front and back sides of leaves, photos of burst pustules, and collection time.
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Domestic *P. sorghi* urediniospores are spherical to subspherical/ovate, **brown wall**, echinulate, **22~35 × 23~34 µm (average 29 × 26 µm)**, teliospores 31~40 × 18~26 µm ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.1). It is distinguished from *P. polysora* through ITS·LSU rDNA·COX3 phylogenetic analysis (same source, 3.2). CPN writes that common rust spores are darker and more round ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Fig. 6).
f6_conditions: High humidity, daytime temperatures 60 to 77 °F (about 16 to 25 °C), **night temperatures 65 to 70 °F (about 18 to 21 °C)**, **leaves wet at least 3 hours**; It does not winter in New York, but is brought in by the wind from the south every year, and completes its life cycle in *Oxalis* in tropical and subtropical regions. It is not transmitted through residues and is therefore unrelated to tillage ([Cornell Common Rust](https://www.vegetables.cornell.edu/pest-management/disease-factsheets/common-rust-of-sweet-corn), Disease cycle). CPN also notes that cool nights and high humidity are more severe in seed-production corn ([CPN Encyclopedia Common Rust](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-rust-of-corn)).) and are associated with 18-49% yield loss under glass conditions ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Introduction).
f7_occurrence: Korea: corn common rust was traditionally considered *P. sorghi*, but in the 2021-2024 national survey (37 samples), *P. sorghi* was only confirmed at 4 locations (3 samples in Gangwon 1992, 1 sample in Buan, Jeollabuk-do, 2021) ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Introduction·3.3·Table 1). There is also a domestic paper on common rust infection in 1978 (search snippet) ([online-rpd 327](https://online-rpd.org/journal/view.php?number=327)).) The first recorded literature in Korea and the plant disease list registration information are unverified. Overseas: EPPO distribution page is 404, CABI is unverified.

f1_names: **Official Korean disease name: unverified.** The new record paper is in English, and the authoritative source of "southern rust" and "southern common rust" could not be found ("corn southern rust" in the quarantine note is a working label). EPPO carries *Puccinia polysora* Underwood (PUCCPY), English name southern rust, brown rust of maize ([EPPO PUCCPY](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PUCCPY), Overview). Since the intermediate host is unknown, it is possible that it is an allopatric parasite, but this has not been confirmed ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Introduction).
f2_parts_stages: Pustules usually appear first in the middle and upper canopy after VT; vegetative-stage occurrence is uncommon except in late-planted corn. Severe disease also affects husks, leaf sheaths, and ear shanks. Younger leaves are more susceptible, and late-planted and double-cropped corn have greater risk (CPN). Korean specimens were collected mainly in September–October, with pustules on both leaf surfaces and rarely on stems (Lee et al. 2025). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust) [Source 2](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/)
f3_symptoms: **Orange to tan pustules, approximately 1/16 in (1.5 mm) in diameter**, mostly on the front of the leaf, with only chlorosis visible on the back. Secondary infection pustules are dense and light green to yellow halo is common. Late telia are brown to black and are first seen in hot spots at the edge of the field ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Symptoms and signs). Hyposporodes in domestic specimens were oval/circular, yellow to brown, and occurred on **both sides of the leaf**, and telia were not observed ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.1 Fig. 2K–Q).
f4_confusions: For comparison with common rust, see CPN Table 1 in Section 16 ④. Late cosporosis resembles tar spot perithecium and may require laboratory confirmation, and Physoderma brown spot, eyespot, Curvularia leaf spot, genetic disorders, and mite damage are also similar ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Diagnosis·Fig. 8–13). In Korea, common rust symptoms observed in Gunwi since 2006 were initially confused between common rust and southern rust (search snippet) ([Nabais et al. 2013](https://repository.pertanian.go.id/items/10443e19-845b-46c3-8556-acde9ae9c092/full)).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* US guidance describes orange pustules about 1.5 mm across, predominantly on upper leaf surfaces, with high density, halos, middle/upper-canopy distribution, and occurrence after VT. Korean *P. polysora* frequently forms pustules on both leaf surfaces, so upper-surface predominance is not a reliable rule in Korea. Lee et al. 2025 considered a 2013 Gunwi report based solely on upper-surface field symptoms to have limited reliability. [Source 1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Request close-ups of both leaf surfaces. Ask about planting date, including late planting, occurrence date (especially September–October), and initial hotspots at field edges. [Source 1](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/)
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Domestic *P. polysora* urediniospores are light brown, oval/sub-spherical, **colorless echinulate walls**, **25~40 × 17~29 µm (average 33 × 24 µm)**, and are longer and larger than *P. sorghi* (brown walls, spherical~ovoid). the uredinia of *P. polysora* are oval, *P. sorghi* is circular. They are divided into separate clades through ITS (bootstrap 99%), LSU (100%), and COX3 phylogenetic analysis ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.1·3.2·Discussion).
f6_conditions: **Infection occurs after about 6 hours of leaf wetting**, and dew is often sufficient. **About 80 °F (27 °C)** and high humidity are advantageous. The incubation period is as short as 9 days, and one pustule produces spores for up to 8 days. Because it requires a living host and cannot survive on remnants, it does not winter in the north and is brought in by wind from the tropics every year. Alert methods such as residue management have no effect ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Disease cycle). The germination rate of urediniospores of domestic isolates was the highest (49%) at 25 ℃, similar at 20-30 ℃, rapidly decreased when the temperature exceeded 32 ℃, less than 2% at 38·40 ℃, and over 40% germinated within 9 hours at 25-28 ℃ ([Lee et al. 2025](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), 3.4 Fig. 6). Fungicide effectiveness is expected when the initial discovery stage is VT~R3, R5 is low, and R6 is absent ([CPN Southern Rust Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-southern-rust), Table 2).
f7_occurrence: Korea: **New domestic record in 2025.** "*P. polysora* is newly reported in Korea and was the prevalent species over *P. sorghi* among the collected samples"([Lee YK et al. 2025, Mycobiology 53(5):637-647, PMID 40792185](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12337728/), Abstract). The collection distribution is 2 in Gangwon, 2 in Chungbuk, 3 in Chungnam, 23 in Jeonbuk, and 3 in Jeonnam. Collection was conducted between September and October 2021 and 2024 (e.g., Jeonju 2021-09-27, Yeongdong 2021-10-16, Hongcheon 2024-09-06, Buan 2024-10-05). There is the National Institute of Agricultural Sciences and the Agriculture, Forestry and Livestock Quarantine Headquarters (same source, 3.3·Table 1). The paper calls this the “first conclusive evidence” of domestic existence (Discussion). As a prior report, a team from Kyungpook National University reported southern rust infection in Jeju and Gunwi field trials in 2008 and 2009 at an academic conference (2013), but the reliability was evaluated to be limited due to the lack of microscopic and molecular evidence ([Nabais et al. 2013](https://repository.pertanian.go.id/items/10443e19-845b-46c3-8556-acde9ae9c092/full), snippet). Domestic quantity damage and occurrence area statistics are unverified. Overseas: It has recently become prevalent in China, and distribution and spread have also been reported in Japan (Lee et al. (quoted from the 2025 Introduction). There is a review that says it was first recorded in West Africa in 1949 and in China since 1972 (search snippet)([PMC11766486](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC11766486/)).) Overseas distribution is not the basis for domestic occurrence.

official_kr_name: Common smut (Nongsaro, under the synonym *Ustilago zeae*)
f1_names: The official name in Korea is **common smut** (黑穗病, Smut), and Nongsaro writes the pathogen as ***Ustilago zeae*** (old synonym) ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), title·pathogen). 『Korean Plant Disease List』 (2004) also lists “common smut (Smut) by *Ustilago zeae*” (second citation) ([Han et al. 2015, Res. Plant Dis. 21(4):280-289](https://doi.org/10.5423/RPD.2015.21.4.280), p.280–281). The EPPO preferred name is *Ustilago maydis* (de Candolle) Corda(USTIMA), synonym *U. mays-zeae*, *U. zeae*, common/boil/blister smut of maize ([EPPO USTIMA](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/USTIMA), Overview). The change in classification to view *Mycosarcoma maydis* as the current name could not be confirmed as a primary source (it only appears in the Commons file name) ([Commons Category](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Ustilago_maydis)).
f2_parts_stages: It occurs on male and female ears, stems, and leaves, and rarely on roots ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), Symptom Description). All actively growing or embryonic tissue is susceptible, and any above-ground area is affected **from seedling to maturity** ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Common Smut·Symptoms; [CPN Common Smut](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-smut-of-corn)).
f3_symptoms: The diseased area abnormally enlarges and becomes a **gall**. The large lump is more than 10 cm in diameter. It is initially covered in a glossy white membrane, but when it bursts, black powder (teliospore) comes out ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), symptom description). Or, it is surrounded by a greenish-white to silvery-white membrane and reaches a diameter of 15 cm when mature, and small hard nodules the size of peas appear on the leaves ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Fig. 1·2). None of the major ear rots produces a lump ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Corn smut).
f4_confusions: Head smut is a seedling systemic infection where the spores are not wrapped in fleshy nodules, so it is only visible during the flowering period ([UNL CropWatch Head Smut](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut)), It is distinguished from common smut by the presence of **tangled filamentous vascular remnants** mixed with telia) ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Head Smut–Symptoms). It is distinguished from ear rots by the presence or absence of galls ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)).) Plants with galls on lower stems appear red in the fall and may be similar to aphid damage ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Common Smut paragraph 3).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Fleshy nodule wrapped in a silver-white membrane, black powder after membrane rupture, site of occurrence (stem, leaf, ear, tassel), size 10-15 cm. If the tassel or spikelet is replaced by a mass of spores and a thread-like vascular tube, it is head smut.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Request a cross-section of a gall. Ask about wounds from detasseling, hail, wind-blown soil, insects, or machinery; nitrogen and manure inputs; and rainfall and temperature during early growth (Illinois RPD 203). [Source 1](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html)
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* teliospores are black, spherical to sub-spherical, superficially spiny, **8-12 µm in diameter** ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Disease Cycle). The range overlaps with head smut teliospore (9~14 µm), so it is difficult to determine based on the microscopic size alone (same source). The source of molecular identification is unknown. Mycotoxin testing is not generally required (no toxins listed in the Corn smut section of CPN Ear Rots). Alternatively, it is described as not toxic to livestock ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), para. 5).
f6_conditions: Illinois: **At the beginning of growth, infection is most severe when there is little rainfall and the temperature is 26-34 ℃**, and teliospore germinates when there is moisture at 10-35 ℃. Dry periods and abnormally low temperatures and high humidity that slow growth are also advantageous, and are abundant in soils rich in nitrogen and organic matter (livestock manure) ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Common Smut) Paragraphs 3 and 4·Disease Cycle). CPN: Excessive nitrogen/livestock manure, herbicide damage, mechanical wounds, relatively dry and warm weather (no values) ([CPN Common Smut](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/common-smut-of-corn)). Nongsaro: Incubation period 7-21 days, only zygotic mycelium of the opposite sex forms nodules ([Nongsaro D00001177](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sKidofcomdtyTabCode=FC&sKidofcomdtyCode=FC040401&sicknsCode=D00001177), Occurrence environment). **Conflict:** Domestic media (quoting data from the Rural Development Administration) reported that "temperatures are 20-30°C in the middle and late stages of growth, occurs frequently when there is a lot of rain, and occurs frequently in the central and southern plains" (search snippet, original text not read) ([Korea Food & Drug Daily](http://www.kfdn.co.kr/61784); [Enriched and Livestock Newspaper](http://www.amnews.co.kr/news/articleView.html?idxno=53928)),) This is the opposite of Illinois' 'little rainfall in the early stages of growth'. It is necessary to check the primary source of domestic reports.

f1_names: **Official Korean name: unverified.** Nongsaro, 『Korean Plant Disease List』 (2004) 2nd citation, web search did not find the Korean name for corn head smut anywhere. “head smut” is a pseudonym. The scientific name is *Sporisorium reilianum*, and the synonyms are *Sorosporium reilianum*, *Sphacelotheca reiliana*, and *Ustilago reiliana* ([PNW Plant Disease Management Handbook: Corn Head Smut](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548), Pathogen). Illinois RPD 203 (1990) uses *Sporisorium holci-sorghi* as the representative name ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), introduction), and CPN uses *Sphacelotheca reiliana* ([CPN Head Smut](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/head-smut-of-corn)).) Pathotypes are differentiated into corn and sorghum lines, and hybrids that infringe on both are also reported ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html)). "f. sp. The primary source listing the name "*zeae*" has not been viewed. The EPPO code was identified as SPHTRE in the quarantine note ([EPPO SPHTRE](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SPHTRE/categorization)).
f2_parts_stages: It occurs on male and fetassels, and rarely on leaves ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html); [PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)). **Infection occurs in the soil during the seedling stage, and symptoms become evident only at the flowering stage**([UNL CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut)), mycelium enters the undifferentiated spike and tassel tissue from the seedling meristem) sori ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Disease Cycle).
f3_symptoms: Sori consist of dark-brown to black teliospore masses initially covered by a thin grayish-white membrane that soon ruptures. Tangled thread-like vascular remnants remain among the spores; infected tassels usually lack pollen. Phyllody and teliospore streaks on leaves also occur (Illinois RPD 203). Wire-like tassel projections, finger-like ear proliferation, teardrop-shaped ears without silks, and dwarfing in some varieties are reported (UNL; PNW). [Source 1](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html) [Source 2](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut) [Source 3](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)
f4_confusions: It is easy to confuse with common smut, and is distinguished by the absence of fleshy lumps and the presence of vascular threads ([UNL CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut); [Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html)).) The possibility of foliar symptoms being confused with other causes such as downy mildews is unverified as there is no source for comparison.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Tassels and ears are replaced by spore masses. Look for wire-brush-like vascular strands in tassels, teardrop-shaped ears without silks, phyllody, dwarfing, and absence of the fleshy galls characteristic of common smut. [Source 1](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548) [Source 2](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html) [Source 3](https://www.ipmimages.org/browse/detail.cfm?imgnum=1265069)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Whether multiple years in the same field (soil teliospore survival 5 to 7 years ([PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)) or more than 3 years ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html))), Infection of all ears on one plant (systemic infection) ([Bugwood 1265069 caption](https://www.ipmimages.org/browse/detail.cfm?imgnum=1265069)), Seed source.
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Teliospores are reddish-brown to black, spherical to subspherical, prominently spiny, and 9–14 µm across; sporidia are colorless and 7–15 µm long (Illinois RPD 203). Size overlaps with common-smut spores. A source for a molecular-identification protocol was not verified. Because occurrence in Korea was not established by the original research, suspected samples require specimen collection and laboratory confirmation. [Source 1](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548) [Source 2](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html) [Source 3](https://www.ipmimages.org/browse/detail.cfm?imgnum=1265069)
f6_conditions: It is infected even at a soil temperature of **15 ℃, and is more likely to be infected at 20-30 ℃ ([PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548), Cause and disease cycle). **Low soil moisture (15-25% w/w)** is optimal for seedling infection, and temperature is more important than soil moisture for infection (part of original sentence damaged). High soil moisture and winter soil temperatures above 0 ℃ lower the survival rate of teliospore, which is abundant in clay loam soils and worsens with nitrogen deficiency ([Illinois RPD 203](http://ipm.illinois.edu/diseases/series200/rpd203/index.html), Last paragraph of Disease Cycle; [CPN Head Smut](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/head-smut-of-corn)). Early sowing can avoid germination temperatures), and seeds are not the main source of infection, but diseases can be introduced through surface spores. There is ([UNL CropWatch](https://cropwatch.unl.edu/plant-disease/corn/head-smut); [PNW](https://pnwhandbooks.org/node/2548)).

f1_names: Nongsaro corn **ear rot**(穗腐病, Ear rot) writes the pathogen as ***Gibberella fujikuroi*** and specifies corn in the text ([Nongsaro D00001173](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173), title·pathogen·environment of occurrence). 『Korean Plant Disease List』 (2004) lists "ear rot caused by *G. fujikuroi*" and "stalk rot caused by *F. moniliforme*" (second citation), and it is said that the *G. fujikuroi* species complex, previously called *F. moniliforme*, was divided into several species. Explain ([Han et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.5423/RPD.2015.21.4.280), p.281). The most common overseas causal pathogen are *F. verticillioides*, *F. proliferatum*, and *F. subglutinans*, and the former two species are related to fumonisin ([UT Crops Fusarium Ear Rot](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/), Causal Species; [CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)). **Caution:** In EPPO Since *G. fujikuroi* is a synonym for the rice bakanae disease bacteria *F. fujikuroi* ([EPPO GIBBFU](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/GIBBFU)) Nongsaro), it is confusing if the scientific name is translated as is. In addition, Annex 3 of the notice adds *Gibberella zeae* to corn “ear rot” (Section 21). The EPPO code of *F. verticillioides* was identified as FUSAVR in the quarantine note. The judgment that Nongsaro ear rot corresponds to overseas Fusarium ear rot is an inference based on symptoms and conditions, and the scientific name reflected in the latest edition of NCPMS/Plant Disease List is unverified.
f2_parts_stages: Infection occurs through silks, insect injuries, and kernel wounds. *F. verticillioides* can also grow systemically through the stalk into the ear (CPN). Disease can continue beyond R6 until kernel moisture falls below 18% (UT Crops). Scouting should begin in late dent (R5). Disease also occurs in storage (Nongsaro). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/fusarium-ear-rot-of-corn) [Source 2](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/) [Source 3](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots) [Source 4](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173)
f3_symptoms: The shell and kernels are partially pink to reddish brown, pink fluffy mold is abundant around bug holes and wounds, and white stripes appear on late-stage infected kernels ([Nongsaro D00001173](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173), symptom description). The grains are discolored **scattered or in groups**, and white, pink, and purple mold is visible, and white stripes caused by fungal growth under the skin are called **'starbursts'**. It often occurs on grains damaged by the European light moth, the common tobacco moth, and birds ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Fig. 5·6; [UT Crops](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/)).
f4_confusions: CPN Ear Rots criteria: Gibberella has pink to red mold and bract and silk adhesion (mummification) starting from the tip of the ear, Aspergillus has olive green powder (aflatoxin) at the tip of the ear, Diplodia has dense white to gray mold and black pycnidia that progresses from the base to the tip, Penicillium has blue-green powder and 'blue-eye' grains (some ochratoxin), and Trichoderma is dark blue-green. Spores and early germination, Cladosporium has black-green grains and black stripes, Nigrospora has black spores that fall off when rubbed ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), each item). The source for differentiation from insect/bird damage itself and physiological grain splitting is unverified. Nongsaro also writes that it is common in fruits with wounds from birds and insects.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Scattered/clustered distribution at grain level, white to pink/purple downy mildew, starburst white stripes, overlap with insect/bird damage areas, start of ear tip (Gibberella differentiation), base start and black pycnidia (Diplodia differentiation), olive green/blue-green shade (Aspergillus/Penicillium differentiation). **Distinguishing the causative species (*F. verticillioides*/*F. proliferatum*/*F. subglutinans*) and determining fumonisin are impossible with photographs.**
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* High temperature/drying before and after seeding, ear damaging pests, hail, Bt traits, harvest delay, storage moisture ([UT Crops](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/); [CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Laboratory tests are often the only reliable method for identifying ear rot·mycotoxins, and **fumonisin levels can be high even when the disease appears superficial** ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Diagnosis·Mycotoxin). It is recommended that moldy corn be tested for toxins before feeding ([CPN Fusarium Ear Rot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/fusarium-ear-rot-of-corn)).) Morphology and EF1α sequence analysis were used to identify domestic FFSC species (case of stump rot) ([Han et al. 2015](https://doi.org/10.5423/RPD.2015.21.4.280), p.281). For comparison of toxin measurement methods, see Section 21, ⑤.
f6_conditions: Nongsaro: **Slightly dry and warm weather**, storage moisture of 18% or less recommended ([Nongsaro D00001173](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?menuId=PS00202&sicknsCode=D00001173), occurrence environment/control method). CPN: High temperature and dryness after the planting season, wind, rainwater splashing and insect spread, overwintering of leftover grasses and weeds (no figures) ([CPN Fusarium Ear Rot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/fusarium-ear-rot-of-corn)); Damage from insects and hail is most severe in warm areas and fields, and fumonisin may increase if the warm period during the planting season overlaps with the wet period before harvest ([CPN Ear Rot) Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Conditions). UT: Most severe above **77 °F (25 °C)** and during wet periods prior to harvest, with optimum fumonisin production below **75 °F (about 24 °C)** ([UT Crops](https://guide.utcrops.com/corn/corn-ear-rots/fusarium-ear-rot/), Favorable Conditions). Field studies showing that drought stress increases rot and FB1 (Parsons & Munkvold) were only confirmed by search snippets ([PMC1240682](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC1240682)).
f7_occurrence: Korea: Nongsaro lists corn ear rot under *G. fujikuroi*, and the 2004 Korean disease list includes it, as secondarily cited by Han et al. 2015. *F. subglutinans* and *F. temperatum* were identified from Korean corn stalk rot in 2013–2014, not from ear rot. Korean ear-rot species composition involving *F. verticillioides* and *F. proliferatum*, and fumonisin contamination, were not verified. New additions to disease-list version 6.1 include corn ear rot/stalk rot caused by *Fusarium vorosii* (Kim et al. 2023, appendix p.341). Overseas: UT describes Fusarium ear rot as the most common corn ear rot in the US. Dominance of *F. verticillioides*, *F. proliferatum*, and *F. meridionale* in Chongqing, China, and Japanese feed-corn counts of 41 *F. verticillioides*, 36 *F. proliferatum*, and 27 *F. fujikuroi* isolates, were based on search snippets. f1_names: The Nongsaro corn document dated 2019-11-28 describes the disease corresponding to Gibberella ear rot and gives *Gibberella zeae* (Schw.) Petch, asexual morph *Fusarium graminearum* Schwabe. Korean Notice Annex 3 uses the generic Korean label ear rot for this pathogen on corn and the Korean label corresponding to Fusarium head blight on small-grain cereals. A secondary citation of the 2004 Korean disease list instead pairs the Korean label with the English name Gibberella stalk rot (Han et al. 2015, p.281). New additions to list version 6.1 include the corresponding corn disease caused by *Fusarium asiaticum* (Kim et al. 2023, p.341). EPPO's preferred name is *Fusarium graminearum* Schwabe (GIBBZE), with synonyms *Gibberella zeae* and *G. saubinetti*; common names include ear rot and stalk rot of maize. Disease names depend on the affected organ and crop. [Source 1](http://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/psb/psbk/kidoContentsFileDownload.ps?kidofcomdtyNo=29198) [Source 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519071) [Source 3](https://doi.org/10.5423/RPD.2015.21.4.280) [Source 4](https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/74bd/f76ea4401b3ad67d867904177e097932fd30.pdf) [Source 5](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/GIBBZE)
f2_parts_stages: Infection begins around silking and continues through harvest and storage; the pathogen overwinters in diseased ears and husks (Nongsaro). Ears are most susceptible 2–6 days after silking. Spores disperse through rain splash and wind; the fungus usually enters through the silk channel. The same pathogen also causes stalk rot in corn and Fusarium head blight in wheat (CPN). [Source 1](http://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/psb/psbk/kidoContentsFileDownload.ps?kidofcomdtyNo=29198) [Source 2](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gibberella-ear-rot-of-corn) [Source 3](https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/AC-52)
f3_symptoms: At harvest time, infection usually begins at the tip of the ear and causes discoloration and rot inside**. During storage, it rots anywhere, and many pink to red mycelium and spore masses are formed between the bracts and the ear. If these ears are used as feed for pigs, etc., they cause poisoning ([Nongsaro Attachment 29198](http://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/psb/psbk/kidoContentsFileDownload.ps?kidofcomdtyNo=29198), 1. symptoms). If there is a lot of mold, the silks and bracts stick to the ear and become **'mummified'**. It is easy to recognize in an intact ear, but it is difficult to identify after shelling ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Gibberella Fig. 8; [CPN Gibberella Ear Rot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gibberella-ear-rot-of-corn)).
f4_confusions: Fusarium ear rot is sporadic, white to pink, purple, starburst at the grain level, and Gibberella is pink to red starting from the tip of the ear. Diplodia (white-grey, black pycnidia), Aspergillus (olive-green), and Penicillium (blue-eye) are also identified ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots)). Gibberella prefers slightly cooler temperatures than Diplodia (search snippet)([OSU C.O.R.N. 2014-36](https://agcrops.osu.edu/newsletter/corn-newsletter/2014-36/potential-corn-ear-rot-and-mycotoxin-problems-ohio)). There is a photo of hail damage on the ears, which may be accompanied by wounds ([CPN Gibberella Ear Rot](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/gibberella-ear-rot-of-corn), photo caption).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Pink to red mold starting from the tip of the ear, adhesion of bracts and silks (mummification), pink mold on the outer tip of the bract, accompanied by hail and insect wounds. After shelling, it is difficult to identify grains alone. **It is impossible to determine species and toxins (DON·NIV·ZEA) in FGSC from photos.**
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Ask about rainfall and temperature during approximately the first 3 weeks after silking, continuous corn, nearby wheat with Fusarium head blight, and harvest delays (CPN). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots) [Source 2](https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/AC-52) [Source 3](https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.07043-11) [Source 4](https://doi.org/10.5423/ppj.oa.12.2023.0173) [Source 5](http://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/psb/psbk/kidoContentsFileDownload.ps?kidofcomdtyNo=29198)
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* Visible mold does not establish toxin concentration. Blacklight testing is unreliable because vomitoxin does not fluoresce. Methods include NIR (rapid, indirect), lateral-flow strips (rapid, mainly qualitative), ELISA (sensitive, semiquantitative), and chromatography (the most accurate quantitative method in the cited account). Zearalenone and aflatoxin require separate tests. OSU gives a rule of thumb against feeding grain with more than 5% moldy kernels; this is source guidance, not a Korean regulatory limit. Korean corn isolate lineages were identified by AFLP: lineages 3 and 7 all produced DON, while 2 and 6 mainly produced NIV (Lee et al. 2012). Korean wheat/barley FGSC isolates were identified by direct TEF-1α PCR and were mainly *F. asiaticum* (Jeon et al. 2024). Nongsaro describes sickle-shaped macroconidia with 3–7 septa, 25–62 × 2.5–5.0 µm; no microconidia; and 10–12 µm chlamydospores. f6_conditions: The optimal temperature for pathogen growth is **24~26℃**, **if there is frequent rain during the pistil formation period**, the occurrence becomes more severe ([Nongsaro Attachment 29198](http://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/psb/psbk/kidoContentsFileDownload.ps?kidofcomdtyNo=29198), Sections 2 and 3). Cool, wet weather in the early season, long-term autumn rainfall that delays harvest, continuous cropping, wheat Fusarium head blight is severe in the origin, abundant in the northern United States and Canada, but rare in the south ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Gibberella; [OSU AC-52](https://ohioline.osu.edu/factsheet/AC-52)). DON production 21-29 ℃, zearalenone 15 Figures such as less than ℃ and grain moisture exceeding 20% are unverified by only checking with search snippets of Iowa State and Purdue data. The value for 3 to 5 days of RH above 95% on the rice Fusarium head blight page does not apply to corn because the crops are different ([Nongsaro paddy rice Fusarium head blight](https://www.nongsaro.go.kr/portal/ps/pss/pssa/sicknsSearchDtl.ps?pageIndex=1&pageSize=10&sicknsCode=D00000753&menuId=PS00202)).) For storage, moisture of less than 18% of ears and less than 15% of seeds is recommended (Section 4 of the Nongsaro document). Zearalenone can be effective at 1 to 5 ppm in feed, and pigs are most sensitive ([CPN Ear Rots](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-ear-rots), Mycotoxin Testing). OSU's FDA advisory level is US standards, not Korean standards.
f7_occurrence: Korea: *F. graminearum* (broadly defined) **568 strains** were collected from corn in eight regions in Korea and analyzed by AFLP. As a result, lineage 7 was 75%, lineages 6 and 3 were 12% each, and lineage 2 was 1%. The authors concluded that lineage 7 may have been introduced relatively recently along with imported corn seeds ([Lee et al. 2012](https://doi.org/10.1128/aem.07043-11), Abstract). The same abstract states that this fungus is an important pathogen of domestic wheat, corn, barley, and rice, and that harvested grains are frequently contaminated with DON and NIV. According to the O'Donnell lineage nomenclature, lineages 2, 3, 6, and 7 correspond to *F. meridionale*, *F. boothii*, *F. asiaticum*, and *F. graminearum* s.s., respectively, but this correspondence was not directly confirmed in the text of Lee et al., 2012. In domestic wheat and barley, *F. asiaticum* was the majority ([Jeon et al. 2024](https://doi.org/10.5423/ppj.oa.12.2023.0173)). domestic corn DON·ZEA monitoring and standard values are unverified. f1_names: **Official Korean disease name: unverified.** Could not be confirmed in NCPMS, List of Plant Diseases in Korea, or QIA list. “Stewart wilting disease” and “Stewart wilt disease” appeared in the search summary, but the source could not be verified. “Corn bacterial wilt disease” in the quarantine note is also a working label. The scientific name is *Pantoea stewartii* subsp. *stewartii*(EPPO ERWIST), synonym is *Aplanobacter stewartii*, *Bacterium stewartii*, *Erwinia stewartii*, *Pseudomonas stewartii*, *Xanthomonas stewartii* ([EPPO ERWIST datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet), Identity). The English name is Stewart's disease, Stewart's wilt, bacterial leaf blight/wilt of maize, jackfruit bronzing (search snippet)([EPPO datasheet PDF](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/download/datasheet_pdf)).
f2_parts_stages: Corn, especially sweet corn, is the main host; the cited host list also includes *Dracaena sanderiana*, *Oryza sativa*, *Saccharum officinarum*, and *Setaria pumila*. Symptoms affect leaves (streaks), stalks (vascular tissue and pith cavities), tassels (early emergence and discoloration), and seed (deep invasion without reaching the embryo). Wilt is particularly important in sweet corn, while the leaf-blight phase occurs after tasseling in dent corn (EPPO). [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet)
f3_symptoms: In the wilt phase, susceptible plants wilt rapidly, pale-green to yellow streaks dry to brown, tassels emerge prematurely and become discolored, and cavities may form in the stalk pith. In the leaf-blight phase after tasseling, streaks begin at corn flea-beetle feeding wounds and entire leaves can become straw-colored (EPPO). Lesions generally follow the veins with wavy margins; pale-yellow bacterial ooze may emerge from cut stalks (CPN). [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet) [Source 2](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/stewarts-disease-of-corn)
f4_confusions: Goss's wilt also produces seedling dieback and lesion, but **freckles** (dark green to black water-soaked spots within the lesion) are found only on Goss's wilt. Stewart's disease has been rarely recorded since the early 2000s, so it is recommended that suspected samples be sent to a diagnostic institution. NCLB is a 1-4 inch cigar-shaped lesion with even edges and no freckles or bacterial leakage ([CPN Goss's Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Look-alikes). For drought and nutrient deficiency, refer to the general criteria in the Goss disease document, which states that there are no freckles, gloss spills, or bacterial spills (same source). No data related to hail and wind injuries was found.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Pale-green to yellow streaks follow leaf veins and have wavy margins. Request close-ups of corn flea-beetle feeding scars at the start of streaks, wilted sweet-corn seedlings, pale prematurely emerged tassels, and longitudinal stalk sections showing pith cavities. [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet) [Source 2](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/encyclopedia/stewarts-disease-of-corn) [Source 3](https://www.agdia.com/company/news/1756576/agdia-releases-immunostrip-for-pstew-pantoea-stewartii-stewarts-wilt)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Variety (whether sweet corn or not), previous winter temperature, corn flea beetle observation, and seed import history. When infected stems and leaves are cut, yellow bacterial ooze comes out, and when the lesion section is viewed under a microscope, bacteria are flowing out from the ducts ([EPPO ERWIST datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet), Detection and inspection).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* EPPO diagnostic protocol of isolation and culture, immunofluorescence, ELISA, conventional/real-time PCR, barcoding, fatty acid profile; The United States recommends ELISA seed health testing for corn seed lots (same source). Agdia "Pstew" ImmunoStrip's performance is unverified by only checking the news title ([Agdia news](https://www.agdia.com/company/news/1756576/agdia-releases-immunostrip-for-pstew-pantoea-stewartii-stewarts-wilt)). regulated quarantine pest), so official confirmation must be made by an official inspection agency such as the Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs Quarantine Headquarters.
f6_conditions: The main insect vector in the United States is the corn flea beetle (*Chaetocnema pulicaria*), which overwinters as an adult and can retain bacteria throughout its life. **If the average daily temperature from December to February is above freezing, insect vectors can survive and a severe outbreak is possible, and if it is below -3℃, a severe outbreak is unlikely** (based on the U.S. surveillance model). If there is a lot of ammonium N and P, susceptibility increases, if there is a lot of Ca·K, it decreases, and high temperatures make the disease worse. Bacteria in seeds disappear after 200-250 days at 8-15 ℃ and 110-120 days at 20-25 ℃ (Guo et al. 1987) Seed → seedling transmission rate is “very low” ([EPPO ERWIST datasheet](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/ERWIST/datasheet), Biology·Phytosanitary measures). The Fahrenheit winter temperature index (sum of monthly average °F for December, January, and February) is <90 usually not occurred, 90 to 100 is moderate, and >100 is usually severe ([Mulrooney 2009, Univ. of Delaware](https://sites.udel.edu/weeklycropupdate/?p=771)). Domestic *C. pulicaria* distribution is unverified, so domestic risk cannot be determined.

Agdia "Pstew" ImmunoStrip's performance is unverified by only checking the news title ([Agdia news](https://www.agdia.com/company/news/1756576/agdia-releases-immunostrip-for-pstew-pantoea-stewartii-stewarts-wilt)). regulated quarantine pest), so official confirmation must be made by an official inspection agency such as the Agriculture, Food and Rural Affairs Quarantine Headquarters.

section_title: Goss’s bacterial wilt and leaf blight — *Clavibacter nebraskensis*
f1_names: **Official Korean disease name: unverified.** Current scientific name is *Clavibacter nebraskensis* (Davis et al.) Li et al.(EPPO CORBNE), synonym is ***Clavibacter michiganensis* subsp. *nebraskensis***, *Corynebacterium michiganense* pv./subsp. *nebraskense*, *Corynebacterium nebraskense*, English name is Goss's wilt, leaf freckles of maize ([EPPO CORBNE](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CORBNE), Overview). Since the Korean examination lists the old academic name, it will be missed if you search only by the current name.
f2_parts_stages: Infection can occur at any growth stage. Infection before V6 is more likely to become systemic and cause wilt and death, with systemic wilt usually first seen at V2–V6. Later infection generally causes leaf blight. Symptoms are most conspicuous after silking (R1). Leaves, vascular tissue, and stalk pith are affected (CPN). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight)
f3_symptoms: The common leaf-blight phase begins as pale-green water-soaked streaks, becoming tan to gray-brown lesions with wavy edges parallel to the veins. Dark-green to black water-soaked freckles within lesions, translucent when backlit, are described as diagnostic of Goss’s wilt. Small orange bacterial-ooze droplets form when wet, leaving a dried-varnish-like sheen after drying. Systemic wilt includes slimy stalk rot, wilting, and discoloration of xylem and stalk pith (CPN). [Source 1](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight)
f4_confusions: CPN look-alikes criteria: NCLB (1 to 4 in cigar shape with even edges, no freckles or bacterial shedding; some hybrids do not produce freckles, making distinction increasingly difficult), Stewart's wilt (distinguished by presence or absence of freckles), bacterial streak disease (*Xanthomonas vasicola* pv. *vasculorum*; Narrower tan to yellow lesions, bright yellow in backlight, no freckles, bacterial shedding possible on both sides), Diplodia leaf streak (bright yellow halo, pycnidia), **nutrient deficiency (N, K, P) and drought/leaf tip die** (no freckles, glossy shedding, or bacterial shedding, drought causes uniform browning from the leaf margins inward) ([CPN Goss's) Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Look-alikes). Ilso is not mentioned (unverified).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Backlit photos of the lesion show translucency of freckles, glossy exudate on the lesion surface, lesion at the edges of the undulations, and discoloration of the vascular bundles on the longitudinal section of the stem. The absence of freckles does not rule out Goss’s wilt (hybrid differences).
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* History of hail, strong winds, and sandstorms, continuous cropping and no-till, occurrence in the previous year, and hybrid name ([CPN Goss's Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Conditions).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* It is easy to be confused with other diseases, so confirmation by a diagnostic institution is recommended, and observation of bacterial leakage from lesion sections is helpful in diagnosis (same source, Diagnosis). The presence or absence of the ImmunoStrip·PCR commercial test and EPPO diagnostic protocol is unverified. Since it is a regulated quarantine pest, official confirmation must be made by an official inspection agency.
f6_conditions: It occurs easily around **27 ℃ (80 °F)** and can be suppressed** above 35 ℃ or below 21 ℃. **Hail, wind, sandstorms, storms** Wounds are entry points and irrigation can help progress but is not required. Survival is granted if you survive **at least 10-15 months** in surface remnants and are buried. Risk factors include susceptible hybrids, reduced tillage, and continuous cropping of fields with a history of occurrence, and alternative hosts include sorghum, Italian ryegrass, sudangrass, foxtails, Johnson grass, and crabgrass. Seeds are not considered a significant means of dispersal ([CPN Goss's Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Conditions).
f7_occurrence: Korea: **Domestic outbreak records unverified** (no entry for Korea in EPPO distribution table; absence not confirmed). Overseas (EPPO, updated on 2026-04-30): US "Present, restricted distribution" (16 states including Colorado, Illinois, Iowa, Nebraska, Texas, etc.), Alberta and Manitoba, Canada (Ontario no longer present), **South Africa "Present, restricted distribution"**, Mexico "Absent, unreliable record", no Asian items ([EPPO CORBNE distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CORBNE/distribution)). CPN records the first observation in Nebraska in 1969 and reports on Mexico (2023) and South Africa (2024) ([CPN Goss's Overview](https://cropprotectionnetwork.org/publications/an-overview-of-gosss-bacterial-wilt-and-blight), Distribution) **Mexican records conflict between CPN and EPPO**, EPPO photo #18117 credits Mexican researchers ([EPPO CORBNE photos](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/CORBNE/photos)).

f1_names: An official Korean disease name was not verified. The pathogen is *Peronosclerospora philippinensis* (W. Weston) C.G. Shaw (PRSCPH), synonym *Sclerospora philippinensis*; the established English name is Philippine downy mildew of maize (EPPO). The older USDA CAPS account lists *P. sacchari* as a synonym and cites isozyme evidence for conspecificity (Yao et al. 1991b). Groben et al. 2026 retained them as separate species: a 62-ortholog phylogeny from 57 specimens, including 17 type specimens, placed their lectotypes in different clades, rejecting older conspecificity arguments based on morphology, host range, and isozymes (Weston 1920; Bonde et al. 1984; Micales et al. 1988). That study treated *Sclerospora northii* as a later synonym and *S. indica* as a possible synonym; it selected Los Baños 1919 specimen BPI 187314 as lectotype and found that BPI 789414, designated as an isotype by Crouch et al. 2022, belonged to *P. sacchari*. Korean and Japanese regulations list the two species separately in the original research. [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PRSCPH/datasheet) [Source 2](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf) [Source 3](https://fuse-journal.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FuseVol17Art12.pdf)
f2_parts_stages: Chlorotic streaks may appear on the first leaf as early as 9 days after sowing. Downy growth on lower leaf surfaces is visible from the second-leaf stage through tasseling and silking. Sporulation emerges through stomata on both leaf surfaces, especially the lower surface, and on leaf sheaths, tassel axes, inflorescences, and chlorotic husks; mycelium colonizes the growing point. Seed may appear normal externally while containing mycelium in the pericarp, embryo, and endosperm (USDA CAPS). [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf)
f3_symptoms: Long chlorotic yellow streaks may affect all leaves, with gray downy growth of conidiophores and conidia on lower leaf surfaces. Leaves become narrow and abnormally erect; tassels and ears become malformed, pollen production declines, ears may fail to develop, and sterility occurs. Early infection causes dwarfing and death. The cited datasheet describes particularly high pathogenicity among corn downy-mildew pathogens, losses of 40–60% in corn, and an 8% nationwide loss in the Philippines in 1974–75. Synergism with maize streak virus (MSV) is reported, and MSV may mask the mildew symptoms (USDA CAPS). [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf) [Source 2](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf)
f4_confusions: Corn downy mildew is caused by up to 10 species of *Peronosclerospora*, *Sclerophthora*, *Sclerospora*, and other downy mildews and **physiological disorders (fertility, weather, etc.)** also cause similar symptoms ([CAPS Corn](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), Easily Confused Pests). The grayish-white dew-like conidial layer in the chlorosis area is a distinguishing mark from physiological disorders, but it can dry out in sunlight and low humidity and become “matted fragments” ([CAPS Small Grains](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.3). The specific differentiation criteria from Zn·Mg deficiency streaks are unverified.
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Long chlorosis stripes that become larger towards the upper leaves, **early morning** grayish-white dew-like growths on the back of the leaves (close-up), narrow, upright leaves, male and female deformity. From photos, it is only possible to determine 'suspicious downy mildew' and the species level is impossible.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Seed origin and import history, proximity to sugarcane and sorghum, disease outbreak period (seedling stage or not) ([CAPS Small Grains](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf), Survey).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* The CAPS-approved method is morphological identification: conidiophores 150–400 µm long with 2–4 dichotomous branches; conidia elongate-ovoid to rounded-cylindrical, 17–21 × 27–39 µm; oospores rare or absent. A comparison table covers *P. maydis*, *P. sacchari*, *P. sorghi*, and *S. rayssiae* var. *zeae* (White 1999, cited by CAPS). Morphology varies with culture conditions, developmental stage, and host; no species-specific PCR was available when that datasheet was written. Groben et al. 2026 found that about half the existing specimens had been misidentified and emphasized type-specimen-based molecular data for diagnostic development. Official confirmation is required for a regulated quarantine pest. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf) [Source 2](https://fuse-journal.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FuseVol17Art12.pdf)
f6_conditions: Conidia are formed at **18~23 ℃**, germinate at 10~35 ℃, and infection rate is highest above 16 ℃ (Bonde et al. 1992). For conidia formation, germination, and infection, **night temperature of 21~26℃**(Dalmacio & Raymundo 1972), high humidity, and **leaf surface water film in the dark for more than 4~5 hours**(Exconde 1970) are required. Conidia cannot germinate when exposed to sunlight, wind, and low humidity for 1 to 2 hours. The number of systemic infections is positively correlated with humidity, spore load, and rainfall, and negatively correlated with temperature and sunlight. If seed moisture is **less than 14%**, there is no seed transmission (Exconde 1976) ([USDA CAPS Corn datasheet](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.2 Biology and Ecology).
f7_occurrence: Korea: **Domestic outbreak records unverified** (no entry for Korea in EPPO table). Overseas (EPPO, updated on 2021-11-25): China (Guangxi, restricted), India (Bihar, Delhi, Maharashtra, Punjab), Indonesia (Sulawesi), Nepal, Pakistan, Philippines, Thailand; South Africa and the United States have an "Absent, unreliable record" ([EPPO PRSCPH distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/PRSCPH/distribution)).
f8_quarantine: Korea: **regulated quarantine pest — *P. philippinensis* and *P. sacchari* separately listed**(+*P. maydis*) (Notice Annex 2 "Fungus *Peronosclerospora philippinensis* (W. Weston) C.G. Shaw" / "*Peronosclerospora sacchari* (T. Miyake) Shirai & Hara")([KR-Notice Appendice 2](https://www.law.go.kr/LSW/flDownload.do?flSeq=169519059)).
