EU: not listed (check)(0 searches for Peronosclerospora/Sclerospora)([EU-2072](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX:02019R2072-20261015)). **USA: deleted from select agent** — There was "Peronosclerospora philippinensis (Peronosclerospora sacchari)" in 7 CFR 331.3(b) in editions 2024-12-16·17, but as of **89 FR 101845 (2024-12-17), it has been removed from edition 2025-01-16** ([eCFR 2024-12-17 Edition](https://www.ecfr.gov/on/2024-12-17/title-7/section-331.3); [eCFR 2025-01-16 Edition](https://www.ecfr.gov/on/2025-01-16/title-7/section-331.3)); APHIS Pests of Concern No. 37 "Philippine downy mildew" remains ([US-PoC](https://www.aphis.usda.gov/laws-regs/animal-plant-diseases-pests-concern)), 7 CFR 319.24 "Sclerospora sacchari") Import of climbing corn seeds and parts from Southeast Asia, Australia, New Zealand, and Japan is prohibited due to “…and other downy mildews” ([US-319.24](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/section-319.24), (a)·(c)). The reason for deletion and the original text of 89 FR are not available for viewing. **Groben et al. The 2026 "Current Select Agent Listing" statement conflicts with this revision and therefore follows the quarantine note (compare eCFR editions).** China: **检疫性有害生物 "Peronosclerospora spp. (non-Chinese) 玉米霜霉病菌（non-Chinese species）"**(genus unit; unverified as there is no definition in the original text whether *P. sacchari* corresponds to "non-Chinese species")([CN](https://assets.ippc.int/static/media/files/reportingobligation/2025/01/07/CATALOGUE_OF_QUARANTINE_PESTS_FOR_IMPORT_PLANTS_TO_THE_PEOPLES_REPUBLIC_OF_CHINA_updated_20241128.doc)). Japan: **検疫有害動植物**(*P. philippinensis*, *P. sacchari*, *P. maydis*, *P. sorghi* respectively)([JP](https://laws.e-gov.go.jp/law/325M50010000073)). Australia: unverified.

section_title: Brown stripe downy mildew — *Sclerophthora rayssiae* var. *zeae*(= *S. zeae*)
f1_names: An official Korean disease name was not verified. EPPO's preferred name is *Sclerophthora rayssiae* Kenneth, Koltin & Wahl (SCPHRZ), with *S. rayssiae* var. *rayssiae* and *S. rayssiae* var. *zeae* Payak & Renfro among other names. Its English common name is brown stripe downy mildew of maize. Groben et al. 2026 use *Sclerophthora zeae*, formerly *Sclerophthora rayssiae* var. *zeae* (p.221). The authority and original publication for that combination, possibly Crouch et al. 2022, were not verified. The barley pathogen var. *rayssiae* is morphologically very similar to var. *zeae* but has a different host range (USDA CAPS, p.5). [Source 1](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SCPHRZ/datasheet) [Source 2](https://fuse-journal.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FuseVol17Art12.pdf) [Source 3](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf)
f2_parts_stages: Lesions appear only on leaves** and do not appear to cause systemic infection. Younger plants are more susceptible and appear first in lower leaves. Hosts include crabgrass (*Digitaria bicornis*, *D. sanguinalis*), sorghum, and corn ([CAPS S. rayssiae](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.1·p.3).
f3_symptoms: It is clearly bordered by a narrow chlorosis/yellow stripe with a width of **3~7 mm** and is divided into leaf veins, and in some genotypes, it turns red to purple. As the lesion grows laterally, stripes and stains become worse, and the lower leafs appear light brown and burnt. A dew-like spore layer appears on both sides of the lesion and disappears when necrosis occurs, and oospores are found only in the mesophyll of necrotic tissue. Yield losses of up to 63% have been reported in India (Payak & Renfro 1967), and incidences of 80-100% have been reported in high altitude areas ([CAPS S. rayssiae](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.3).
f4_confusions: Unlike other downy mildews, it has no abnormalities in the fire or vegetative organs and its leaves do not tear. Corn rice dwarf (crazy top, *Sclerophthora macrospora*) has male foliage and excessive tillering, and corn downy mildew (*P. sorghi*) has chlorosis, dwarfing, white stripes, narrow and straight leaves, and foliage. Physiological disorders can produce similar symptoms, and zinc deficiency can predispose to infections ([CAPS S. rayssiae](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.1·p.3·p.5).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Photograph lesions beside a ruler: vein-delimited streaks 3–7 mm wide, red/purple/brown discoloration, progression from lower leaves, no leaf shredding, normal tassels, and no systemic dwarfing. Using lesion width and color plus absence of malformation and dwarfing to make a preliminary distinction from systemic Philippine/sorghum downy mildew and crazy top with phyllody is an inference in the original research. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf) [Source 2](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf)
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Dew-like growth on both sides of leaves on **cool, humid mornings** (usually disappears in the afternoon), rainfall, soil temperature, occurrence of crabgrass, seed origin ([CAPS S. rayssiae](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf), p.4 Survey).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* CAPS-approved morphological identification uses sporangia measuring 18.5–26 × 29–66.5 µm, borne in groups of 2–6 on short determinate hypha-like stalks, germinating by releasing zoospores; oospores measure 29.5–37 µm. By contrast, *Peronosclerospora* conidia germinate by germ tubes. This obligate biotroph does not grow on artificial media. The 2016 datasheet reported no available serological or molecular diagnostic methods and noted development of an NPDN SOP. Current molecular methods using cox2, ITS, or other markers were not verified by the original research. [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf) [Source 2](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Peronosclerospora-philippinensis-small-grain-manual-datasheet.pdf)
f6_conditions: Sporangia form at 22–25 °C and release zoospores at 20–22 °C; zoospores germinate at 15–30 °C. Oospores are more abundant above 28 °C (Payak 1975). Soil temperatures of 28–32 °C favor disease. The cited account describes low incidence with annual rainfall of 4–60 cm, intermediate incidence at 60–100 cm, and high incidence at 100–200 cm. Zoospore infection requires 12 hours of leaf wetness. Primary inoculum consists of oospores in soil residue, surviving up to 4 years (Singh 1971a); secondary spread occurs through rain splash and contact, with a maximum trapping distance of 1.65 m. Seed transmission is below 1% (Lal & Prasad 1989); transmission does not occur after storage for more than 4 weeks at seed moisture below 14%. The pathogen can overwinter in crabgrass (USDA CAPS). [Source 1](https://caps.ceris.purdue.edu/wp-content/uploads/2025/07/Sclerophthora-rayssiae-var-zeae-corn-manual-datasheet.pdf)

section_title: Maize lethal necrosis — MCMV (*Machlomovirus zeae*) + a coinfecting virus in the family Potyviridae (e.g., SCMV)
f1_names: An official Korean disease name was not verified; the Korean working labels in the original notes were informal. Maize lethal necrosis (MLN) results from synergistic coinfection with maize chlorotic mottle virus (MCMV) and another cereal-infecting virus in the family Potyviridae, such as SCMV, MDMV, or WSMV. These are not all members of the genus *Potyvirus*: WSMV belongs to *Tritimovirus*. MCMV is associated with species *Machlomovirus zeae* (EPPO MCMV00; Tombusviridae), synonym Maize chlorotic mottle machlomovirus. EPPO gives *Potyvirus sacchari* for SCMV (SCMV00) and *Potyvirus zeananus* for MDMV (MDMV00). Johnsongrass mosaic virus isolates may also be associated with MLN in East Africa (Prasanna et al. 2020). [Source 1](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/) [Source 2](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/MCMV00) [Source 3](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf) [Source 4](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SCMV00/distribution) [Source 5](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/MDMV00) [Source 6](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943)
f2_parts_stages: From the seedling stage to maturity, **all growth stages are susceptible** ([CIMMYT Causes & Symptoms](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)),) The earlier the infection, the greater the damage and the entire harvest may be lost if infected early in the growing season ([CIMMYT MLN portal](https://mln.cimmyt.org/); [CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), p.1).
f3_symptoms: Early symptoms are mosaic and chlorotic mottling, followed by necrosis beginning at leaf margins, death of the growing point (dead heart), premature husk drying, and poorly filled or sterile ears. SCMV alone causes mild mosaic/mottling; MCMV alone can cause shortened internodes, severe chlorotic mottling, and leaf necrosis (CIMMYT flyer). Kenya's first report describes mottling spreading from the base of young whorl leaves toward their tips, necrosis progressing from margins to midribs, and dead heart (Wangai et al. 2012, Plant Disease 96:1582; search snippet only, full text HTTP 403). MCMV-only severity varies with genotype, infection stage, environment, isolate, and coinfecting viruses; MLN is generally more severe (CDFA). Reported losses in affected Kenyan counties in 2012–2013 were 23–100%; national losses in 2013 were approximately 500,000 tonnes (US$180 million) (Prasanna et al. 2020). [Source 1](https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf) [Source 2](https://www.apsnet.org/publications/plantdisease/2012/October/Pages/96_10_1582.3.aspx) [Source 3](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf) [Source 4](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943)
f4_confusions: MCMV or SCMV alone are usually mild, but together they produce a rapid synergistic effect ([CIMMYT Causes & Symptoms](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)),) MCMV alone can also cause significant losses ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), Abstract). Therefore, it is not possible to definitively distinguish between MCMV alone and MLN using only photos (inference). The only reference to confusion with drought, trace element deficiency, and stem moth damage is low-quality secondary data (SlideShare, original text not available) ([SlideShare](https://www.slideshare.net/slideshow/mln-disease-and-its-management-2015/55609041)). Standard for differentiation from nitrogen deficiency (lower leaf V-shaped yellowing), MSV, and domestic report MYMV). Primary data was not found (unverified).
f5_differentiation:
*Features assessable in photographs:* Chlorosis spots (proximal) at the base of young leaf blades, necrosis progressing from the leaf margin to the midrib, dead heart (stem longitudinal section), early drying of bracts, poor ear filling, distribution within the field (more at the margins in the Kenyan report). In the final necrosis stage, photographic judgment is impossible due to MCMV alone, drought, and nutrient stress.
*Additional photographs, questions, and field checks:* Density of thrips, leaf beetles, and aphids, seed source (imported or not), continuous cropping and absence of a fallow season, surrounding grasses and weeds ([CIMMYT Flyer](https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf); [CIMMYT Causes](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)). **ImmunoStrip** detects leaf juice antigens within 30 minutes and can be used by non-experts, so it is used for field surveys ([CIMMYT MLN Diagnostic Techniques](https://mln.cimmyt.org/mln-diagnostic-techniques/)).
*Features requiring laboratory tests:* DAS-ELISA (leaf·insect vector·seed identification test), PCR/RT-PCR, LAMP (same source). RT-PCR is more sensitive than ELISA, NGS is only available in specialized diagnostic laboratories, and **SCMV is highly variable, so serological results may be inconsistent** ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), 4. MLN diagnostics). The report that seed RT-PCR/RT-qPCR is more than 3,000 times more sensitive than commercial ELISA is a search snippet ([Bernardo et al. 2023](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC9901749/)). **Confirmation of MLN requires detection of MCMV and potyvirus respectively**([CIMMYT Diagnostic Techniques](https://mln.cimmyt.org/mln-diagnostic-techniques/)). MCMV is a regulated quarantine pest, so official confirmation is required.
f6_conditions: MCMV is transmitted by thrips and leaf beetles, and potyvirus is transmitted by aphids. There is also mechanical transmission through infected/contaminated seeds, infected soil/remnants, and agricultural machinery ([CIMMYT Causes](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)). MCMV insect vectors are leaf beetles such as corn rootworms in the central United States, and corn thrips *Frankliniella williamsi* in Hawaii ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), p.1). Seed transmission rates vary between sources: approximately 0.03–0.04% in the early United States ([CIMMYT Causes](https://mln.cimmyt.org/causes-symptoms/)), <0.04% (Jensen et al. 1991)·Kenya 0.059% ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), paragraph 66), **approximately 0.004%** (cultivation test over 85,000 grains, Bernardo et al. 2023; The virus is mainly found in the pericarp and pedicel, but not in the embryo and endosperm) ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), p.1). CIMMYT recommends a two-month corn-free season, legume crop rotation, weed removal, and a ban on using infected field seeds, suggesting that continuous cropping and year-round cultivation are risk factors ([CIMMYT Flyer](https://mln.cimmyt.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/39/2016/06/MLN-FLYER-final-complete.pdf)). **Temperature and humidity thresholds not found (unverified).**
f7_occurrence: Korea: **MCMV, SCMV, and MLN all have domestic occurrence records unverified.** There is no Korea in the MCMV distribution of CABI 2026 (CDFA cited) and Prasanna 2020, and there is no Korea in the EPPO SCMV Asia distribution (including Japan, Taiwan, and China) ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), Worldwide Distribution; [EPPO SCMV00 distribution](https://gd.eppo.int/taxon/SCMV00/distribution)). absence) It has not been confirmed. For MDMV, there is a paper on genetic analysis of resistance by domestic researchers in 1985, but the abstract does not mention whether the inoculum was a domestic isolate or whether it occurred domestically ([Heo et al. 1985](https://www.koreascience.kr/article/JAKO198530710155411.page)). New reports of domestic corn viruses include Maize yellow mosaic virus, unrelated to MLN (check only the title) ([Plant Disease PDN](https://apsjournals.apsnet.org/doi/10.1094/PDIS-11-17-1767-PDN)). Overseas: MCMV first reported in Peru (1974), later in the United States (Kansas corn lethal necrosis), Argentina, Thailand, Mexico, China, Kenya (first detected in September 2011), Uganda, Rwanda, Democratic Republic of Congo, Ethiopia, Taiwan, Ecuador, Spain ([Prasanna et al. 2020](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.virusres.2020.197943), Introduction). CIMMYT lists Kenya, Ethiopia, Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda, Democratic Republic of Congo, and Burundi as confirmed countries, but the text is inconsistent as it says "six eastern African nations" ([CIMMYT MLN portal](https://mln.cimmyt.org/); [MLN Distribution](https://mln.cimmyt.org/mln-distribution-and-spread-in-africa/)).) Overseas records are unrelated to domestic situations or regulatory status.

US: not select agent, official regulatory table unverified([US-331](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-7/section-331.3)). Australia: unverified. **Conflict:** The CDFA PRP notes that Korea is not on the USDA PCIT's list of MCMV harmful organism countries ([CDFA PRP](https://blogs.cdfa.ca.gov/Section3162/wp-content/uploads/2026/07/Maize-chlorotic-mottle-virus-_ADA_PRP_-with-citations.pdf), Official Control), but the Korean notice designates MCMV as a regulated quarantine pest. It appears that the PCIT did not reflect the Korean exam, and the original text of the PCIT was not confirmed as 403.
